lead: Printed transmission lines are copper strips made on a dielectric board. A microstrip has a top strip and a bottom ground plane; a stripline hides the strip between two grounds; a coplanar line puts the strip and side grounds on one face. These lines guide microwave fields in a flat, cheap, repeatable layer instead of a metal pipe. Their effective permittivity εeff sets characteristic impedance Z0, guided wavelength λg and phase velocity, so the same board can hold matching sections, filters and feeds for MIC and MMIC circuits.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for Z0 and wavelength, and Chapter 1.3 for line impedance and electrical length.

blocks.text: A microstrip is a strip conductor of width W on a dielectric substrate of thickness h, with a continuous ground plane on the other side. The dielectric has relative permittivity εr (dimensionless). Fields travel in the substrate and in the air above the strip. Because the two media differ, the wave is quasi-TEM: it looks like TEM at low frequency, but a small longitudinal field remains.

A stripline is a strip buried in a homogeneous dielectric between two ground planes. All fields stay in one dielectric, so it supports pure TEM and εeff = εr. A coplanar waveguide (CPW) places a centre strip and two side grounds on the same top surface; the fields cross the narrow gaps. CPW needs no backside ground for the microwave path, which helps in monolithic circuits. Some syllabi call these printed transmission lines.

Field confinement improves as frequency rises. At low frequency the fields spread several substrate thicknesses into air; at high frequency they crowd under the strip. εeff is the weighted permittivity seen by the wave. It lies between 1 (air) and εr: 1 ≤ εeff ≤ εr. It sets phase velocity vp = c/√εeff and guided wavelength λg = λ0/√εeff, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and λ0 the free-space wavelength.

Z0 is characteristic impedance in ohms; 120π Ω ≈ 377 Ω; ln is the natural logarithm; W/h is dimensionless. Use W and h in the same unit.

items: Choose εr and h from the substrate data sheet, and choose the target Z0, often 50 Ω.
Guess W/h, then compute εeff from the first formula.
Compute Z0 from the second formula; adjust W until Z0 is close to the target.
Check that W is manufacturable and that loss and dispersion are acceptable.

blocks.text: For W/h < 1, other standard closed forms apply; do not use the wide-strip formula outside its range. In stripline, εeff = εr and a wider strip lowers Z0. In CPW, Z0 falls as the gap narrows or W rises.

sections.h3: Loss, dispersion and use in MIC and MMIC

blocks.text: Three loss mechanisms matter. Conductor loss comes from the finite conductivity of copper. At high frequency current flows in a thin skin depth δ = √(2/(ω μ σ)), where ω = 2πf is angular frequency, μ is permeability and σ is conductivity. Resistance per metre rises roughly as √f. Dielectric loss comes from substrate loss tangent tan δ; it rises with frequency and with field in the substrate. Radiation loss comes from the open top of microstrip and from bends and discontinuities; it grows at high frequency and on thick, low-εr substrates.

Dispersion means εeff, Z0 and vp change with frequency. Microstrip is not pure TEM, so short pulses and wideband signals distort; the effect grows as h becomes a noticeable fraction of λg. Skin effect and surface roughness add conductor loss. A good design keeps h small, uses a low-loss substrate, and avoids sharp discontinuities.

Printed lines are the wiring of microwave integrated circuits (MICs) and monolithic microwave integrated circuits (MMICs). A MIC puts separate chips and printed passives on a substrate; an MMIC puts transistors and lines on one semiconductor die. Microstrip and CPW make matching sections, filters, couplers and bias lines. Stripline gives good shielding when both sides can be grounded. See Unit 4 for MMIC technology and Unit 3 for patch antennas, which are built on the same substrate.

examples.question: A microstrip has εr = 4.4, h = 1.6 mm and W = 3 mm. Find W/h, εeff and Z0. Use the wide-strip formulas.
steps: W/h = 3 mm / 1.6 mm = 1.875, dimensionless. Since W/h ≥ 1, the wide-strip formulas apply.
examples.check:
import math
er = 4.4
h = 1.6e-3
W = 3.0e-3
r = W / h
eeff = (er + 1) / 2 + (er - 1) / (2 * math.sqrt(1 + 12 * h / W))
z0 = 120 * math.pi / (math.sqrt(eeff) * (r + 1.393 + 0.667 * math.log(r + 1.444)))
print(round(r, 3))
print(round(eeff, 2))
print(round(z0, 1))

traps: Using εr instead of εeff in λg and vp; the wave sees air plus dielectric, so it travels faster than a wave in bulk dielectric.
Calling microstrip pure TEM. It is quasi-TEM and has dispersion; stripline in a homogeneous dielectric is the pure-TEM printed line.
Mixing up microstrip and stripline: microstrip has air above the strip; stripline has the strip buried between two ground planes.
Putting W and h into a ratio formula with different units, or treating W/h as if it had units. Only the dimensionless ratio enters.
Ignoring skin effect, dielectric loss and radiation loss at high frequency; conductor loss rises roughly as √f and radiation grows on thick, low-εr substrates.

quiz.q: Define effective permittivity εeff of a microstrip.
quiz.a: εeff is the equivalent relative permittivity seen by the quasi-TEM wave. It lies between 1 and εr, and sets vp = c/√εeff and λg = λ0/√εeff.

quiz.q: Why is microstrip called quasi-TEM rather than pure TEM?
quiz.a: Its fields lie partly in air and partly in the substrate. The dielectric-air boundary adds a small longitudinal field component, so it is not pure TEM, though it is close at low frequency.

quiz.q: A microstrip has εr = 4.4 and W/h = 2. Estimate εeff and Z0 with the wide-strip formulas.
Why does dispersion matter for a wideband microstrip line?
quiz.a: εeff varies with frequency, so Z0 and vp vary. Different spectral components get different delays, so pulses distort. The effect is worse at millimetre waves and when h is a noticeable fraction of λg.

quiz.q: Which printed line has εeff = εr, and why?
quiz.a: Stripline. The strip is buried in a homogeneous dielectric between two ground planes, so all the field is in one dielectric and εeff = εr.

quiz.q: Name three loss mechanisms in microstrip and state their frequency trend.
quiz.a: Conductor loss rises roughly as √f through skin effect. Dielectric loss rises with frequency and tan δ. Radiation loss rises with frequency and is stronger on thick, low-εr substrates.

quiz.q: Give two reasons CPW is used in MMIC circuits.
quiz.a: The strip and side grounds are on the top surface, so series and shunt elements are easy to connect without backside processing. The ground is close to the strip, which suits compact monolithic layouts; ground vias and loss still need care.

beyond: Not for the exam. Printed lines now include substrate-integrated waveguide (SIW), where rows of vias make a waveguide-like channel in the same board, and gap waveguide for millimetre waves. Flexible printed lines appear in phone antennas and wearable RF tags. Research searches: 'microstrip dispersion model', 'conductor surface roughness loss', 'coplanar waveguide MMIC', 'substrate-integrated waveguide transition'. The same εeff idea returns in metamaterial and slow-wave lines.
